case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Reversing in part a permanency order, the Court held the circuit court lacked authority to order the Department of Human Services to pay the cost of transporting a child for post-permanency visitation with his psychological parents, and certainly not for years past his eighteenth birthday.
key_cases.relevance: It constrains judicially created spending obligations on the child-welfare agency, a point of intersection with audit and appropriations oversight.
key_cases.quote: the circuit court had no authority to order the DHS to pay transportation costs for such visitation with psychological parents after permanency was achieved, let alone after A.E. turned eighteen

key_cases.case_name: Taylor v. West Virginia Department of Health & Human Resources
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment on the retaliatory discharge, Human Rights Act and false light claims of two discharged DHHR lawyers but reversing as to their Whistle-blower Law claims, the Court held that an employer's proffer of an arguably legitimate reason does not entitle it to summary judgment when the motive for the discharge is genuinely disputed.
key_cases.relevance: The underlying dispute concerned a DHHR contract award, the kind of transaction audits examine.
key_cases.quote: There is little question that whether petitioners were discharged for retaliatory or discriminatory reasons is replete with disputed issues of material fact which must be resolved by the fact-finder

key_cases.case_name: West Virginia Regional Jail & Correctional Facility Authority v. A.B.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: On rehearing the Court restated West Virginia's public-entity immunity framework and held the agency immune from vicarious liability for an employee's acts outside the scope of employment, and immune as to discretionary functions unless the plaintiff shows a violation of clearly established law or fraudulent, malicious or oppressive conduct.
key_cases.relevance: It shapes the financial exposure, and therefore the accountability, of state child-welfare agencies.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the WVRJCFA is entitled to immunity for respondent's claims based on vicarious liability for D. H.'s acts

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
key_cases.holding: Reversing a jury verdict and ordering the action dismissed, the Court held that qualified or statutory immunity turns on whether the conduct violated a constitutional or statutory right that was clearly established at the time, and that the plaintiff produced no affirmative evidence of improper motive or intent to harm sufficient to reach a fact-finder.
key_cases.relevance: Immunity doctrine sets the financial exposure that audit and oversight findings can actually be converted into, and this case consolidates that doctrine for West Virginia.
key_cases.quote: we follow a two-part test: (1) does the alleged conduct set out a constitutional or statutory violation, and (2) were the constitutional standards clearly established at the time in question?
